definition: A general-purpose processor with a few dozen to a few hundred powerful cores, built to run varied, branchy code with low latency. In an AI server it is the host that boots the system, runs the operating system and feeds the GPUs.
The adapter that connects a server or GPU to the network. AI servers typically pair one 400–800 Gb/s NIC with each GPU for the scale-out fabric; SuperNICs and DPUs are more capable kinds of NIC.
A transformer neural network with billions to trillions of parameters, trained on large text corpora to predict the next token. Chat assistants, coding tools and AI agents are built on LLMs.

The main memory technology in computers: each bit is stored as charge in a tiny capacitor that must be refreshed many times a second. HBM, DDR, LPDDR and GDDR are all DRAM, packaged and connected differently.

The extended fifth generation of high-bandwidth memory, with pins at roughly 8–10 Gb/s on a 1,024-bit interface (about 1–1.2 TB/s per stack) and stacks of up to 12 dies (36 GB). It is the memory in Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra GPUs.

The sixth generation of high-bandwidth memory (JEDEC standard published in 2025), which doubles the interface to 2,048 bits per stack and moves the base die toward a logic process. It is the memory in NVIDIA Rubin and AMD MI455X.
The 32-bit floating-point format (8 exponent bits, 23 mantissa bits). AI training keeps master weights and many accumulations in FP32 while doing most matrix maths in lower precision.

A 16-bit floating-point format with 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits. It holds more precision than BF16 but a much narrower range, so training in FP16 needs loss scaling; BF16 largely replaced it.

The Open Compute Project's 4-bit microscaling format: blocks of 32 FP4 values share one 8-bit power-of-two scale. NVIDIA's NVFP4 uses smaller 16-value blocks with a finer FP8 scale; AMD and others support MXFP4.
Scientific and engineering simulation on supercomputers (weather, physics, chemistry), historically in 64-bit precision. It was the first market for NVIDIA's datacenter GPUs and for InfiniBand.
Trillions of operations per second, usually integer (INT8) operations; the headline metric for NPUs and edge AI chips. It is not directly comparable with FLOPS quoted at a floating-point format.
The semiconductor standards body that defines memory standards such as DDR, LPDDR, GDDR and HBM, so that chips from Samsung, SK hynix and Micron interoperate.
